prompt: How does hydrogen-bonding affect the O–H stretching absorption of an alcohol in the IR spectrum?

choices.text: Unassociated alcohols show a fairly sharp band near 3600 cm^−1; hydrogen-bonded alcohols show a broader band at 3300 to 3400 cm^−1
Hydrogen-bonded alcohols show a fairly sharp band near 3600 cm^−1; unassociated alcohols show a broader band at 3300 to 3400 cm^−1
choices.why: It's the other way around: the sharp band near 3600 cm^−1 belongs to unassociated alcohols.

choices.text: Hydrogen-bonding moves the O–H band down to about 1050 cm^−1, where it overlaps the C–O stretch
choices.why: The C–O stretch is the band near 1050 cm^−1. The O–H stretch stays in the 3300 to 3600 cm^−1 range.

choices.text: Hydrogen-bonding has no effect; every alcohol shows the same sharp O–H band at exactly 3350 cm^−1
choices.why: The exact position of the O–H stretch depends on the extent of hydrogen-bonding.

explanation: Alcohols show a characteristic O–H stretching absorption at 3300 to 3600 cm^−1, and its exact position depends on hydrogen-bonding. Unassociated alcohols give a fairly sharp band near 3600 cm^−1; hydrogen-bonded alcohols give a broader band at 3300 to 3400 cm^−1 (3350 cm^−1 for cyclohexanol).

prompt: Near what wavenumber does the strong C–O stretching absorption of an alcohol appear, in cm^−1?
explanation: Alcohols have a strong C–O stretching absorption near 1050 cm^−1, in addition to the O–H stretch at 3300 to 3600 cm^−1.

prompt: A compound's IR spectrum shows a broad absorption at 3500 cm^−1 and bands at 1500 and 1600 cm^−1. Which compound fits best?

choices.text: Phenol
Cyclohexanol
choices.why: Cyclohexanol has an O–H band (3350 cm^−1) but no aromatic ring, so it lacks the 1500 and 1600 cm^−1 aromatic bands.

choices.text: Toluene, C6H5CH3
choices.why: Toluene has aromatic bands but no –OH group to give the broad 3500 cm^−1 absorption.

choices.text: Cyclohexane
choices.why: Cyclohexane has neither an –OH group nor an aromatic ring.

explanation: Phenols show a characteristic broad IR absorption at 3500 cm^−1 due to the –OH group, as well as the usual 1500 and 1600 cm^−1 aromatic bands. In phenol itself, monosubstituted-ring peaks also appear at 690 and 760 cm^−1.

prompt: Cholesterol, an alcohol, is converted into 5-cholesten-3-one, a ketone. How could IR spectroscopy show that the reaction worked?

choices.text: The –OH absorption disappears and a C=O absorption appears
A new –OH absorption appears near 3600 cm^−1
choices.why: The product is a ketone with no –OH group, so the –OH absorption should vanish, not appear.

choices.text: The C=O absorption of the starting material disappears
choices.why: Cholesterol has no C=O group. The C=O absorption is new in the product.

choices.text: No change is expected, because IR can't tell alcohols from ketones
choices.why: The O–H stretch at 3300 to 3600 cm^−1 is characteristic of alcohols, so its loss is easy to see.

explanation: The starting alcohol shows an O–H stretch at 3300 to 3600 cm^−1; the ketone product has no –OH but has a C=O group. Success shows up as disappearance of the –OH absorption and appearance of a C=O absorption (Exercise 17.11.1).

prompt: The ^13C NMR spectrum of cyclohexanol shows signals at 69.5, 35.5, 25.9, and 24.4 δ. Which signal belongs to the carbon bonded to the –OH?

choices.why: This is carbon 2, next to the alcohol carbon. Carbons bonded to –OH usually absorb at 50 to 80 δ.
This is carbon 4, across the ring from the –OH, near a typical alkane value.
This is carbon 3, two carbons from the –OH, near a typical alkane value.

explanation: Carbons bonded to the electron-withdrawing –OH group are deshielded and absorb at lower field than typical alkane carbons, mostly in the range 50 to 80 δ. In cyclohexanol, carbon 1 absorbs at 69.5 δ; carbons 2, 3, and 4 absorb at 35.5, 24.4, and 25.9 δ.

prompt: In the ^1H NMR spectrum of an alcohol, where do hydrogens on the oxygen-bearing carbon absorb?

choices.text: 50 to 80 δ
choices.why: That is the ^13C range for alcohol carbons, not a ^1H range.

choices.text: 7 to 8 δ
choices.why: That is where aromatic-ring protons absorb.
That is where 1-propanol's CH3 and middle CH2 protons absorb (0.93 and 1.56 δ). The –CH2O– protons are farther downfield, at 3.58 δ.

explanation: Hydrogens on the oxygen-bearing carbon are deshielded by the electron-withdrawing effect of the nearby oxygen, and their absorptions occur in the range 3.4 to 4.5 δ.

prompt: Why is spin–spin splitting usually not seen between an alcohol's O–H proton and the protons on the neighboring carbon?

choices.text: Acid-catalyzed exchange of the O–H proton is so fast that the splitting is removed
The O–H proton is too far from the C–H protons for them to couple
choices.why: The O–H and neighboring C–H protons can couple: in DMSO, where exchange is slow, splitting is seen.

choices.text: Hydrogen-bonding makes the O–H signal vanish from the spectrum entirely
choices.why: The O–H signal is still there, just unsplit. It disappears only when D2O is added.

choices.text: The electronegative oxygen atom cancels out any coupling to it
choices.why: The cause is rapid proton exchange, not electronegativity.

explanation: Spin–spin splitting is not usually observed between the O–H proton and neighboring protons on carbon. Most samples contain small amounts of acidic impurities, which catalyze exchange of the O–H proton on a timescale so rapid that the effect of spin–spin splitting is removed.

prompt: How can you identify the O–H absorption in an alcohol's ^1H NMR spectrum?

choices.text: Add a little D2O: the O–H proton is exchanged for deuterium, and its absorption disappears
Add a little D2O: the O–H absorption splits into a doublet
choices.why: Exchange with D2O replaces the O–H proton by deuterium, which removes the signal rather than splitting it.

choices.text: Add a little D2O: the absorptions of the protons on the oxygen-bearing carbon disappear
choices.why: Only the acidic O–H proton exchanges rapidly. The C–H protons stay.

choices.text: Add a little acid: the O–H absorption becomes a sharp triplet
choices.why: Acid speeds up proton exchange, which removes splitting rather than creating it.

explanation: If a small amount of D2O is added to the NMR sample, the O–H proton is rapidly exchanged for deuterium and the hydroxyl absorption disappears from the spectrum, which identifies its position.

prompt: In the ^1H NMR spectrum of 1-propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH, the –CH2O– protons at 3.58 δ couple with the neighboring –CH2– protons but not with the O–H proton. Into how many peaks is their signal split?
explanation: The –CH2O– protons have two neighboring –CH2– protons, so the n + 1 rule gives 2 + 1 = 3 peaks: a triplet at 3.58 δ (Figure 17.11.3). Rapid exchange removes any coupling to the O–H proton.

prompt: In the alpha-cleavage pathway of an alcohol in the mass spectrometer, what forms?

choices.text: A neutral radical and a resonance-stabilized, oxygen-containing cation
Water and an alkene radical cation, 18 mass units lighter than M^+
choices.why: That is the other pathway, dehydration.

choices.text: A hydroxyl radical and a carbocation that contains no oxygen
choices.why: Alpha cleavage breaks a C–C bond nearest the –OH group, so the oxygen stays in the cation.

choices.text: An oxygen-containing radical and a cation made only of carbon and hydrogen
choices.why: The charge stays with the oxygen-containing fragment, which is resonance-stabilized.

explanation: Alcohols fragment in the mass spectrometer by alpha cleavage and by dehydration. In alpha cleavage, a C–C bond nearest the hydroxyl group is broken, yielding a neutral radical plus a resonance-stabilized, oxygen-containing cation.

prompt: In DMSO solvent, exchange of the O–H proton is slow, and it couples with the C–H protons on the neighboring carbon. Into how many peaks is the O–H signal of 2-propanol, (CH3)2CHOH, split?
explanation: The oxygen-bearing carbon of 2-propanol carries one hydrogen, so the O–H signal is split into 1 + 1 = 2 peaks, a doublet (Exercise 17.11.2).

prompt: In DMSO solvent, what multiplicity would the O–H signal of 1-methylcyclohexanol have?

choices.text: Singlet
Doublet
choices.why: A doublet needs one hydrogen on the oxygen-bearing carbon, as in cyclohexanol. 1-Methylcyclohexanol's alcohol carbon has none.

choices.text: Triplet
choices.why: A triplet needs two hydrogens on the oxygen-bearing carbon, as in ethanol.

choices.text: Quartet
choices.why: A quartet would need three hydrogens on the oxygen-bearing carbon.

explanation: In DMSO the O–H proton couples with the hydrogens on the neighboring (oxygen-bearing) carbon. In 1-methylcyclohexanol, a tertiary alcohol, that carbon has no hydrogens, so the O–H signal is a singlet (Exercise 17.11.2).

prompt: Why aren't the ^1H NMR absorptions of a phenol uniquely diagnostic for phenols?

choices.text: Its ring protons (7 to 8 δ) and O–H proton (3 to 8 δ) absorb where other kinds of protons also absorb
Its O–H proton never appears in the spectrum, and its ring protons absorb at 3.4 to 4.5 δ
choices.why: Phenol O–H protons absorb at 3 to 8 δ, and aromatic-ring protons near 7 to 8 δ.

choices.text: Its ring protons absorb at 50 to 80 δ, overlapping with alcohol carbons
choices.why: 50 to 80 δ is a ^13C range. Aromatic-ring protons absorb near 7 to 8 δ.

choices.text: Its O–H proton always appears as a sharp triplet that looks like a CH2 group
choices.why: Rapid exchange usually removes O–H splitting. The real problem is the overlap of chemical-shift ranges.

explanation: Phenols, like all aromatic compounds, show ^1H NMR absorptions near 7 to 8 δ, and phenol O–H protons absorb at 3 to 8 δ. In neither case are these absorptions uniquely diagnostic for phenols, since other kinds of protons absorb in the same range.

prompt: 1-Butanol has M^+ = 74. At what m/z does the peak from dehydration (loss of water) appear?
explanation: Dehydration eliminates water (18 mass units), giving an alkene radical cation at 74 − 18 = 56 (Figure 17.11.4).

prompt: Alpha cleavage of 1-butanol (M^+ = 74) gives a peak at m/z = 31. What is the mass of the neutral radical lost?
explanation: 74 − 31 = 43, a propyl radical, C3H7. Breaking the C–C bond nearest the –OH leaves the resonance-stabilized CH2OH+ cation at m/z = 31 (Figure 17.11.4).
